title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
gist: Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged Russian data centers at Yandex, Sberbank, VKontakte and the Finance Ministry, prompting plans for underground facilities and a Putin decree reserving 10 percent of data center capacity for the state. Putin also authorized possible use of foreign data centers, reversing the sovereign internet logic.

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone strikes have degraded or knocked out data centers run by Yandex, Sberbank, VKontakte and the Russian Ministry of Finance, damaging facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupting cloud services for millions of users.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Data centers are now active targets, a new physical risk factor for AI and cloud infrastructure in conflict zones.

insights.claim: Strikes disrupted payment and digital banking apps, e-commerce, video streaming, ride-hailing and food delivery, showing Russia's hyper-centralized system is vulnerable in wartime.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Concentration in a few providers amplifies outage impact.

insights.claim: Yandex was forced to relocate all three of its main supercomputers after drone strikes on the AI data centers housing them.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Russian domestic AI compute capacity is disrupted and costly to rebuild under sanctions.

insights.claim: Russia has been targeting Ukrainian data centers specifically since late September, alongside near-nightly drone and missile attacks on Ukrainian cities.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Both sides now treat digital infrastructure as a military target.

themes.theme: Russian response: underground and state control

insights.claim: Rostelecom raised moving some data centers underground in talks with Norilsk, and a regional governor proposed building data centers in open-pit coal mines with green parks above as camouflage.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Hardened or underground data centers may become a niche demand driver in war-risk regions.

insights.claim: On November 2, Putin signed a decree requiring data center operators to set aside 10 percent of available space and capacity for possible government needs.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: State-reserved capacity effectively taxes commercial compute and signals Kremlin concern about infrastructure vulnerability.

insights.claim: The decree lets a government commission authorize use of foreign data centers in consultation with the FSB, a notable break from the Sovereign Internet Law that had blocked Russian companies from using cloud infrastructure abroad.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Signals wartime pragmatism is overriding digital sovereignty doctrine.

insights.claim: Ukraine's decentralized digital services have proved more resilient despite years of attacks, as the government dispersed energy and telecom nodes and buried more infrastructure underground.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Distribution and hardening is the proven design pattern for resilient digital infrastructure.

insights.claim: Amazon and Microsoft helped Ukraine migrate government resources to cloud regions elsewhere in Europe shortly after the February 2022 invasion, and Ukraine uses Starlink terminals funded by the US, Poland and Germany as backup communications.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler and satellite providers have become part of national resilience strategy.
